svg.title: Five item VPWS design checklist: MTU, failure detection, redundancy, multicast and spanning tree
svg.desc: Five rows. MTU, where the label stack shrinks the usable frame and large packets are dropped silently. Failure detection, where the pseudowire is down but the customer keeps sending. Redundancy, where a single pseudowire plus a single PE is a single point of failure. Multicast, where customer PIM floods across the pseudowire and saturates the circuit. Spanning tree, where port-based mode passes BPDUs and merges two sites into one domain. Each row gives the symptom of ignoring the item and the concrete design action, and a note at the bottom says the spanning tree item is the one that is decided by accident if nobody decides it on purpose.
svg.text: Five things to settle before the VPWS contract is signed, not after
Every row is a support case that is cheaper to prevent than to debug across two organisations
ITEM
HOW IT FAILS WHEN IGNORED
WHAT THE DESIGN MUST DO
MTU
the label tax
Ping works, the file transfer stalls. The label stack ate bytes
nobody budgeted for, so large frames vanish mid-path.
Verify CE and PE MTU end to end, and remember that
tunnels inside tunnels shrink it again. Clamp MSS if needed.
Failure detection
silence ≠ up
The pseudowire is down, the CE keeps sending, and the routing
protocol keeps believing the path is fine.
OAM (CFM/LFM) or BFD, with a timer shorter than the
application’s tolerance. Test it by pulling one link.
Redundancy
one wire, one risk
A single pseudowire over a single PE pair is a single point
of failure dressed up as a service.
Dual PE with dual pseudowires, or the carrier’s protection
switching time written into the contract as a number.
Multicast
someone else’s flood
VPWS does not understand multicast, so it forwards it. Customer
PIM then floods across the pseudowire and fills the circuit.
Estimate the multicast load before signing, or keep multicast
on the Layer 3 side where it can be pruned.
Spanning tree
the decision nobody makes
Port-based mode passes BPDUs, so two sites become one tree.
Root election crosses the WAN and paths become unpredictable.
Filter BPDUs at the CE and keep two domains, or accept the
merge knowingly. Do not let it happen by default.
Item five is the only one that happens even when nobody chooses it. The service is transparent by default; STP convergence is not.
Write the answer into the design document as a sentence: spanning tree does, or does not, cross this WAN.
